## Six digital fraud typologies hitting financial institutions hardest right now, and why real-time decisioning works best alongside your investigators


October is Cybersecurity Awareness Month and we’re committed to helping financial institutions strengthen cybersecurity and build more secure, resilient digital banking experiences. Throughout the month, we’ll be sharing insights, resources and perspectives to support the ongoing work of staying ahead of evolving threats.


A fraud manager at a credit union once told me about a running joke on his team. Whenever he goes on vacation, he says he should just tell the fraudsters because something always happens while he’s gone. People laugh when he tells it. Then they nod, because they have seen it too.


Consider how that plays out. An attack starts at 11:48 p.m. on the Saturday of a holiday weekend, inside a mobile banking session. By the time an analyst opens the alert on Tuesday morning, the money has been gone for more than two days.


I’ve written before about[how financial institutions](https://www.unit21.ai/blog/a-finger-in-the-wind-how-institutions-decide-which-crimes-to-ignore) prioritize fraud investigations, and how it is usually a staffing decision – rarely solely based on risk. A holiday weekend makes staffing decisions like this visible.


The losses behind this are large. The[Federal Trade Commission](https://www.ftc.gov/) (FTC) says consumers reported losing $16 billion to fraud last year, the highest figure it has ever recorded. The[FBI’s Internet Crime Complaint Center](https://www.ic3.gov/) (IC3) counted $20.9 billion in cybercrime losses in 2025.


### What is digital fraud, and why is it different?


Digital fraud is any fraud that begins or ends inside a digital channel – an online banking login, a mobile application (app) session, a profile change, an instant payment. What sets it apart is time. It happens in seconds, usually through a session that looks legitimate, and many digital[payments](https://www.alkami.com/digital-banking-solutions/business-banking/payments/) are hard or impossible to pull back once they clear.


For decades, fraud operations followed a simple sequence. You detected something, you investigated it, and then you tried to recover the money. That sequence made sense when money moved slowly. Digital banking has shortened the window for intervention. If a suspicious transfer is not identified until the next day, the funds may already be gone, leaving little opportunity for recovery.


Artificial Intelligence (AI) widens the gap further. In 2025, the[FBI’s Internet Crime Complaint Center (IC3)](https://www.ic3.gov/AnnualReport/Reports/2025_IC3Report.pdf) tracked AI-enabled fraud as its own category for the first time, counting more than 22,000 complaints and nearly $893 million in losses. Meanwhile, the[Federal Reserve](https://www.frbservices.org/wp-content/uploads/2026-risk-officer-survey.pdf) Financial Services 2026 Risk Officer Report found that 71% of financial institutions still rely on manual review to spot money mule accounts. The fraudsters have automated a good part of their work, while most reviews are still done by hand.


### What are the six digital fraud typologies financial institutions face most often?


When we talk with[banks](https://www.alkami.com/banks/) and credit unions, and when we review the latest public data, six typologies keep coming up. Real attacks rarely stick to one tactic. They chain two or three together, so it helps to understand each on its own.


1. **Account takeover (ATO).** A criminal gets hold of a real account holder’s credentials and logs in as them.[TransUnion](https://www.transunion.com/report/top-fraud-trends) found the suspected ATO digital fraud rate rose 37% from 2024 to 2025.
2. **Peer-to-peer (P2P) and instant payment fraud.** When a payment settles in seconds, the only chance to stop it is before it is sent.
3. **Impersonation scams.** The real account holder logs in and approves the payment themselves, so login controls see nothing unusual.
4. **Elder financial exploitation.** People age 60 and older reported losses of more than $7.7 billion to the[IC3](https://www.ic3.gov/AnnualReport/Reports/2025_IC3Report.pdf) in 2025.
5. **Money mules.** The[Federal Reserve](https://www.frbservices.org/wp-content/uploads/2026-risk-officer-survey.pdf) report found that 49% of financial institutions discover mule activity only after the losses have happened.
6. **Account opening fraud.** Synthetic or stolen identities open accounts that look clean, and weeks later those accounts start working as mules.


Let us consider how the chain works. A scammer calls an older account holder and says they are from the financial institution’s fraud department. The account holder, trying to be helpful, reads back a one-time code, and now it is an account takeover. The scammer adds a new payee, and the money leaves by instant payment to an account opened three weeks earlier with a synthetic identity.


That is four typologies operating in tandem in about ten minutes, and a next-day report has no chance of preventing it. At the end of the chain is a real person who assumed their financial institution was watching, and who was right to expect their accounts to be safeguarded.


### Why does real-time decisioning matter for digital fraud?


Real-time decisioning looks at each digital event (a login, a new payee, a payment) at the moment it happens, and returns an action before the event completes. The financial institution can step in while the money is still in the account, including at 2 a.m. when no analyst is at a desk.


What makes real-time decisioning useful is that it has more than one answer. If the event looks normal, it passes, and the account holder feels nothing. If something seems off, it can ask for step-up authentication, or hold the transaction until a person can review it. If the risk is clear, it blocks the event.


Most legitimate account holders never notice any of this. Friction appears only where the risk is, and the investigators get time back.


### How does the Alkami and Unit21 integration work?


Alkami’s Digital Banking Platform sends events such as logins, account updates, and transactions to[Unit21](https://www.alkami.com/integration/unit21/) in real time. Unit21’s rules engine checks each event against rules the financial institution writes itself and returns an action right away: pass, step-up authentication, or block. Anything flagged lands in one place for investigation.


I want to dwell for a moment on the fact that the financial institution writes the rules. Every financial institution’s account holders, products, and appetite for risk are different. A transaction is just data, and a fraud team should be able to flag whatever pattern matters to them without filing a ticket with a vendor and waiting for an answer. For example, a team might write rules like these:


- A transaction more than 200% above the account holder’s 60-day average triggers step-up authentication.
- Three unique IP addresses on one account within an hour trigger a block.
- An account holder who joined less than six months ago logs in from both an Android phone and an iPhone, and the account goes to review for possible takeover.


Detection gets you an alert, and every alert still needs a decision. Unit21’s AI agents help investigators work through those alerts faster, and document the rationale behind those decisions in a way that supports compliance reviews and audits.


### What results are financial institutions seeing with Alkami and Unit21?


Financial institutions using Alkami digital banking and Unit21 are seeing measurable improvements in[fraud prevention](https://www.alkami.com/fraud-prevention/) , including lower fraud losses, fewer false positives, and faster detection of account takeover and after-hours attacks. Customer results show how these capabilities can help fraud teams stop more suspicious activity while reducing the volume of alerts they need to investigate.


[Service Credit Union](https://www.unit21.ai/customers/service-credit-union) was dealing with as many as 10 to 20 successful account takeovers a day, and fraudsters were completing the theft in under five minutes. After moving to Unit21, the credit union reduced fraud losses by 70% and now prevents more than $1 million in fraud losses every quarter.


[Kinecta Federal Credit Union](https://www.unit21.ai/customers/kinecta-federal-credit-union) caught $70,000 in fraud over a single weekend using shared fraud consortium signals, in exactly the window fraudsters count on. Kinecta also cut its daily alerts from more than 100 to fewer than 50 while doubling true positives.


“We went from over 100 alerts a day to fewer than 50, and nearly half are now truly actionable,” said Jorge Cortes, VP of Enterprise Risk at Kinecta.


### How should financial institutions measure digital fraud outcomes?


There are two things to consider when it comes to. First, how much fraud you stopped before it settled, and second, how much friction you put in front of legitimate account holders along the way. Without both, it is hard to defend the investment to leadership, and harder still to tune the rules with any confidence.


When fraud leaders ask me what to track, I suggest four measures, taken before and after going real time:


1. Losses prevented before settlement, counted in dollars rather than alerts.
2. Step-up and block rates, as a share of all digital events.
3. The false positive rate on stepped-up or blocked events, so you know what your friction is costing.
4. After-hours coverage, i.e., the share of interventions that happened outside staffed hours.


I would look at the fourth one first. It tells you how much of your fraud program works only when someone is in the office.


### How can financial institutions get started this Cybersecurity Awareness Month?


Start with one typology and one metric you trust. Run the rules in the background first and measure what they would have caught, and only then turn on step-up and block actions. Once it works on account takeover, expand to scams, mules, and account opening.


In practice, that looks like this:


1. **Map your digital events.** Document what your digital banking platform already captures, such as logins, device changes, payee additions, and payments.
2. **Pick one typology.** Account takeover is usually the right place to begin, because the signals are clear and the losses are real.
3. **Test before you enforce.** Run new rules against historical data, then in shadow mode on live events, so you can see what they would have caught before they touch a single account holder.
4. **Set your thresholds,** and decide where step-up ends and block begins.
5. **Review the rules every month.** Fraudsters adapt, and your rules need to keep up with them.


There is one question I’d encourage you to ask any vendor, including Unit21, to show what its rules would have caught during the last holiday weekend. A good vendor should be able to answer that with specifics.


Fraudsters already work in real time, weekends included. Every financial institution has to decide whether its defenses will keep the same hours.

### FAQs


1


What is the most common type of digital fraud at financial institutions?


Account takeover is the one financial institutions describe to us most often, and it is growing quickly. TransUnion reported a 37% rise in the suspected ATO digital fraud rate from 2024 to 2025. It is often the first link in a chain that ends with a P2P transfer to a mule account.


2


How is real-time fraud prevention different from transaction monitoring?


Transaction monitoring reviews activity after it happens, often in scheduled batches, to find patterns worth investigating. Real-time fraud prevention decides during the event, returning pass, step-up, or block before the money moves. Most financial institutions need both, one to stop losses and the other to find the patterns behind them.


3


Does real-time fraud prevention create friction for account holders?


When it is set up well, very little. Most digital banking events pass without any interruption, so good account holders never know it is there. Step-up authentication appears only when something looks unusual, and blocks are kept for clear risk. Tracking false positive rates is how a fraud team keeps that friction low.


4


Why are older account holders targeted so often?


Older adults often have more savings, and some are less familiar with how digital scams work. People age 60 and older reported more than $7.7 billion in losses to the FBI’s IC3 in 2025. Behavioral signals, such as a first large transfer to a new payee, are among the best early warnings.


5


What is a money mule, and why should financial institutions care?


A money mule is a person whose account is used to move stolen funds, often without realizing it. The Federal Reserve found that two-thirds of mule fraud involves legitimate account holders who were deceived. Mule accounts are how stolen money leaves the system, so catching them breaks the chain.
